screens.narratorSegment: Debugging smart contracts is different from debugging regular apps because transactions execute on the EVM and you can’t step through them with a traditional process debugger. In this lesson you will learn two complementary approaches: quick in-contract inspection using the console log facility, and deep investigation using Hardhat’s built-in transaction debugger and verbose traces. You will see how console-style prints let you confirm variable values and control flow during a failing test, while stack and transaction traces point to the exact line and call path that caused a revert. We’ll also cover the practical commands you run locally, the meaning of common trace lines, and typical pitfalls such as misreading gas errors or leaving state mutated between tests. By the end you’ll know when to use simple prints and when to rely on a full trace, and you’ll have practiced the diagnostic steps that turn a mysterious revert into a precise fix. Consider what kind of information you want first: a fast value check or a full execution history — that choice shapes the debugging path.

Practice steps to verify fixes

01 — Console placement

Print inputs, intermediate calculations, and the value right before a failing require to see exactly what caused the check to fail.

Mnemonic: print-before-and-after

screens.title: Why debugging on-chain differs
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contracts run on the EVM and their execution is transaction-based, so you can’t attach a conventional debugger to an on-chain process. That means your debugging toolbox must adapt: you need ways to observe values during a transaction and to reconstruct the execution history after a failure. Hardhat addresses both needs. It hosts a local EVM where tests and scripts run quickly, and it augments Solidity with a console logging utility that prints to your terminal during test execution. When a transaction reverts, Hardhat also produces a stack trace showing the sequence of function calls and the file and line where the revert occurred. For deeper analysis, the network can output a full transaction trace with every EVM opcode and gas usage, giving you a step-by-step replay. A practical takeaway is this: start with fast, low-overhead inspections like console prints to narrow suspect code paths. If those prints don’t reveal the root cause, escalate to stack traces and then to a verbose transaction trace to inspect opcodes and gas accounting. A common misconception is assuming an "out of gas" message always means your algorithm is expensive; sometimes a require consumed remaining gas and produced a revert. Always check the stack trace before concluding performance issues. How would you decide which tool to use first on a failing test?

keyIdea.text: Local EVM plus console logging and traces replace process debuggers for smart contract development.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Why debugging on-chain differs
Definition

Execution model matters

Transactions are atomic, stateful, and run in the EVM. You inspect their behavior by replaying or instrumenting them locally rather than attaching a live debugger.

Local inspection

Use Hardhat Network to run tests and scripts locally for fast iteration.

Post-mortem traces

Stack and transaction traces reconstruct execution after a revert.

Analogy

Think of console logs as short roadside markers that show where you passed, and traces as a full GPS replay of the trip. Both are useful; which one you need depends on how far off course you are.

When to print
  • Quickly confirm a variable or branch is reached.
  • Check inputs and immediate outputs.
When to trace
  • Reverts with deep call paths or unclear causes.
  • Out-of-gas or low-level EVM behavior needs opcode detail.
Misconception
Not every gas message means expensive code; check the trace for an earlier revert.
Pro tip
Start with targeted prints then escalate to traces if prints stop short of revealing the cause.
Key takeaway
Choose tools by how much execution history you need to see.

screens.title: Using console.log inside Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat provides a simple debugging utility you can use directly inside Solidity: the console log import. After importing the console helper from Hardhat, you can call the print facility to output values to the terminal when running tests on Hardhat Network. This works much like printing in JavaScript: you can log strings and common types such as uint and address to observe state at specific moments in a transaction. The recommended pattern is to add prints right before a suspected failing check and immediately after calculations so you can see input, intermediate, and post-check values. Keep in mind console logs are intended for development only — they require the Hardhat environment and should not be left in production deployments. A common mistake is assuming console output is part of the transaction receipt; it is not. It appears in the running Hardhat terminal and interleaves with test output. Use console logs for quick hypothesis checks: if a printed value already shows the problem, you can often fix the logic without running a verbose trace. But if prints stop before revealing the cause, escalate to stack traces and verbose traces.

keyIdea.title: Console.log (Solidity)
keyIdea.text: Import hardhat/console.sol and print values from Solidity while running tests locally to inspect execution.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Using console.log
Import and example
// contracts/BuggyContract.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

import "hardhat/console.sol";

contract BuggyContract {
  uint public value;
  function setValue(uint _newValue) public {
    console.log("Current value before update:", value);
    console.log("New value proposed:", _newValue);
    require(_newValue < 200, "Value must be less than 200");
    value = _newValue;
    console.log("Value after update:", value);
  }
}
The printed lines will appear in the terminal running Hardhat tests. Use them to confirm variable values and whether code reached a particular branch.
Quick rules
  • Import hardhat/console.sol only for tests and local runs.
  • Do not ship console imports to production build pipelines.
  • Print values before checks to see why a require fails.
Common mistake

Expecting console output in a transaction receipt — it only appears in the running Hardhat terminal or test output stream.

Key Takeaway

Console logging is the fastest way to check values, but use it only while developing locally.

screens.title: Example: setValue and visible console output
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete example so you can see console logging in action. Imagine a setValue function that logs the current value, the proposed new value, and the updated value. When you call it with a value that violates a require, you will see only the logs emitted before the require; any logs after the failing require don’t appear. In a test run you will notice log lines interleaved with test output, showing the printed values before failure. For example, calling setValue with 250 will print the current and proposed values and then the test output will show a revert with the reason string. This pattern helps you determine whether the error comes from the inputs, a calculation, or the require check itself. A frequent confusion is seeing logs and assuming state changed on-chain — remember the logs are local test output and state only persists if the transaction succeeded. Use console prints to confirm an assumption, then use a stack trace to point exactly at the failing line if prints don’t fully explain the issue. Example: setValue and visible console output means printed logs before a failing require reveal input and intermediate values, helping isolate the failing condition.. In practical terms, walk through a failing setvalue call and the printed output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Example: setValue
Test snippet
// test/BuggyContract.js
it("Should revert if value is too high and show console logs", async function () {
  console.log("--- Testing setValue revert ---");
  await expect(buggyContract.setValue(250))
    .to.be.revertedWith("Value must be less than 200");
  console.log("--- setValue revert test complete ---");
});
When running npx hardhat test you will see printed lines like Current value before update: 100 and New value proposed: 250, followed by the revert message. These prints show what the contract saw before it reverted.
Observation

If you see the proposed value matches your expectation, the require triggered correctly and the issue is the guard condition; if the proposed value is unexpected, look earlier in the call sequence.

Check

If logs stop before a point you expected, the transaction reverted earlier — move prints earlier to narrow the exact failing statement.

Key Takeaway

Console logs reveal the last successful observation before a revert — use them to narrow where the transaction failed.

screens.title: Running tests and reading Hardhat output
screens.narratorSegment: Running your test suite is the normal entry point for debugging. Start with npx hardhat test. If a test fails and you used console prints, you’ll see those prints interleaved with Mocha and Hardhat test output in your terminal. If a transaction reverts, Hardhat will usually print an automatic stack trace showing where the revert happened. The practical process is: first run tests normally and observe printed logs. If you see a revert with a reason string, note the at-line that Hardhat prints; it includes the file name and line number. Second, if the cause remains unclear, rerun the same failing test with npx hardhat test --verbose to obtain a transaction trace with opcode-level detail. Third, when troubleshooting interactive state or running multiple steps, consider launching npx hardhat node and using the Hardhat console to invoke functions manually, inspect storage variables, and replay sequences that lead to the failure. A common mistake is skipping awaits in tests, which can make logs appear out of order or tests pass incorrectly. Always await transactions and deployments. This process ensures you escalate only as necessary, saving time while still giving you deep visibility when you need it.

screens.title: Generic reverts and divide-by-zero
screens.narratorSegment: Not all reverts come with a clear reason string. Some operations, such as a division by zero or an arithmetic error, produce a generic revert without a reason. When that happens, console logs can show you whether the divisor or operand values are what you expect, but if logs don’t show the failing operation, you need to inspect the stack trace. Hardhat’s stack trace will still point you to the file and line that triggered the revert, which is the primary clue to the underlying operation that failed. For example, if you call a divideByZero function with a 0 divisor, the transaction will revert and Hardhat will give a trace showing the divide instruction location. A common misconception is assuming a generic revert is always a compiler or EVM bug; usually it’s caused by an arithmetic or low-level operation in your code. If the failing line is inside an external call, trace the call stack to find the external contract and debug it similarly. The practical approach is first confirm inputs with console logs, then read the at-line in the stack trace, and finally escalate to verbose opcode traces when the issue involves low-level EVM behavior or unexpected gas consumption.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Generic reverts
Problem

Some runtime failures emit a generic revert without a reason string. Division by zero is a common example.

Use console logs

Print the operands involved in arithmetic operations to confirm which value is zero or invalid.

Read stack trace

Find the at-line to locate the exact operation that reverted.

Example
function divideByZero(uint _divisor) public view returns (uint) {
  return value / _divisor; // revert if _divisor is 0
}

// Test
await expect(contract.divideByZero(0)).to.be.reverted;
If console prints show the divisor as zero, the blame is the caller. If the divisor looks valid, follow the stack trace to detect earlier corrupting state or external calls that changed values.

screens.title: Hardhat's transaction debugger & stack traces
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat enhances failing transactions with stack traces that reveal the sequence of function calls leading to a revert, including file names and line numbers. When you see an at-line such as contracts/BuggyContract. sol:21:9, the file and line tell you where the failing statement lives. The call stack shows which functions called which, helping you locate which caller passed a bad input or which nested call failed. The stack trace is your first stop after a revert because it points directly at the code location needing inspection. To interpret it, open the referenced file at the given line and examine the expression or require. Then trace backwards through the call stack to identify the caller that produced the input or state leading to the failure. Remember: the stack trace reports where the runtime error was detected, not necessarily where the original bad data was introduced. Use console logs in callers or earlier states to find where incorrect values were created. A common misunderstanding is thinking the topmost at-line is always the root cause; it’s the symptom location — you must use the call stack and prints to find the originating action.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Transaction Debugger
Reading the trace
Error: VM Exception while processing transaction: reverted with reason string 'Value must be less than 200'
    at Contract. (contracts/BuggyContract.sol:21:9)
    at Context. (test/BuggyContract.js:12:5)
Open the file at the line reported and inspect the statement. If the failing line is inside a nested external call, follow earlier at-lines to find the original caller that passed the problematic value.
Practical checklist
  • Locate the at-line file and line number.
  • Read the surrounding code to identify the failing condition or opcode.
  • Trace backwards through call stack entries to find the origin of bad input.
Misconception

The at-line indicates where the revert was detected, not always where incorrect data originated.

screens.title: Verbose transaction traces (--verbose)
screens.narratorSegment: When a failing transaction involves low-level behavior, unexpected gas consumption, or complex state changes, rerun your tests with npx hardhat test --verbose to produce a full transaction trace. The verbose trace shows every EVM opcode executed, gas costs per opcode, and changes to memory and storage. This level of detail is useful when diagnosing out-of-gas errors that are not simple require checks, investigating subtle storage overwrites, or verifying that external calls behaved as expected. Reading a verbose trace requires patience: look for the point where gas drops or where a REVERT opcode appears, then map that opcode back to the Solidity code using the line numbers and opcodes as clues. A practical approach is to first identify the failing Solidity line from the standard stack trace, then use the verbose opcode trace to inspect the precise EVM operations around that line. Remember that opcode traces are dense; use them as a microscope after your higher-level prints and traces have narrowed the suspect area. This staged escalation ensures you only dive into opcodes when necessary, saving time while still giving you the full fidelity needed to diagnose low-level issues.

screens.title: Using npx hardhat node and the Hardhat console
screens.narratorSegment: For exploratory debugging you can start a local persistent node with npx hardhat node and then use the Hardhat console to interact with deployed contracts manually. This is useful when you want to step through a sequence of transactions, inspect storage between calls, or reproduce a failing scenario by invoking transactions one at a time. The typical flow is: launch the node, deploy your contracts to it through a script or by deploying from the console, then use the console prompt to call functions, check public storage values, and observe return values or reverts. Manual calls let you narrow down the problem by isolating a single step rather than running the whole test. Keep in mind calls from the console still run on the local EVM; console. log output from Solidity will appear in the node terminal, not the console where you type commands. A common pitfall is forgetting that the node persists state across console sessions, so remember to reset state or redeploy when you need a fresh environment. Interactive debugging is especially helpful for complex multi-step flows and for understanding how external contract interactions behave in isolation.

screens.title: Common debugging pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: There are several common pitfalls that slow down debugging. First, misinterpreting gas errors: an apparent out-of-gas can actually come from a require or revert that consumed remaining gas. Always inspect the stack trace before concluding a performance issue. Second, test state leakage: if your beforeEach doesn’t reset state properly, leftover state from a prior test can change behavior unexpectedly. Make sure each test deploys fresh contracts or otherwise resets shared state. Third, missing awaits: forgetting to await an asynchronous ethers. js call can cause subsequent steps to execute with unresolved promises, producing confusing failures or interleaved logs. Fourth, external call failures: when your contract calls another contract and the external call fails, the stack trace might show the revert inside the external contract; you must debug that dependency similarly. The practical strategy is to follow a checklist: run isolated tests, add prints to callers and callees, read the stack trace to find the failing line, and use verbose traces only if the cause remains unclear. Keeping these traps in mind will prevent many false leads and save debugging time. Common debugging pitfalls means check stack traces before assuming gas problems; reset state between tests; always await promises; debug external contracts when needed.. In practical terms, misread gas errors, test state leakage, missing awaits, and external call failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Activity: Debug BuggyCalculator with console.log

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Hands-on: BuggyCalculator
Starter contract
// contracts/BuggyCalculator.sol
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;
import "hardhat/console.sol";
contract BuggyCalculator {
  uint public result;
  function add(uint a, uint b) public {
    console.log("Entering add. a:", a, "b:", b);
    uint sum = a + b;
    require(sum != 100, "Sum cannot be 100!"); // intentional bug
    result = sum;
  }
}
Activity steps
  1. Run npx hardhat test and observe the failing add test and revert message.
  2. Add console logs around sum calculation and re-run to see printed values.
  3. Read the stack trace to confirm the require line and remove it.
  4. Re-run tests to verify the fix.
Key Takeaway

This activity practices the full debug loop and shows when to use prints vs traces.

fullNarratorScript:
Debugging smart contracts is different from debugging regular apps because transactions execute on the EVM and you can’t step through them with a traditional process debugger. In this lesson you will learn two complementary approaches: quick in-contract inspection using the console log facility, and deep investigation using Hardhat’s built-in transaction debugger and verbose traces. You will see how console-style prints let you confirm variable values and control flow during a failing test, while stack and transaction traces point to the exact line and call path that caused a revert. We’ll also cover the practical commands you run locally, the meaning of common trace lines, and typical pitfalls such as misreading gas errors or leaving state mutated between tests. A short hands-on activity will guide you to introduce an intentional bug, capture logs, read the trace, fix the code, and rerun tests. By the end you’ll know when to use simple prints and when to rely on a full trace, and you’ll have practiced the diagnostic steps that turn a mysterious revert into a precise fix. Consider what kind of information you want first: a fast value check or a full execution history — that choice shapes the debugging path.

In this chapter you will gain four practical debugging skills. First, you'll learn how to use the in-contract console print facility to inspect values and confirm execution flow during tests. I’ll show how console statements appear in your test output and how to place them to narrow down problems quickly. Second, you’ll use Hardhat Network’s transaction debugger to read automatic stack traces and identify the exact file and line where a revert occurred. Third, you’ll interpret full transaction traces produced with the verbose flag to inspect opcodes, gas costs, and state changes when a simple print isn’t enough. Fourth, you will learn common pitfalls and strategies — things like misreading gas errors, test state leaking between runs, and forgetting awaits — and how to avoid them. Each objective is practical: we’ll pair demonstration code, tests, and a hands-on activity so you practice observing console output, reading a trace, and making a targeted fix. By the end you will be able to choose the right tool for a problem and follow stepwise diagnostics to resolve complex contract failures.

This second objectives panel focuses on practical verification and common checks you should perform. You will place console prints before and after suspicious operations to check whether execution reaches a line, and to capture values that clarify why a check failed. You will run tests normally and then rerun failing tests with the verbose flag to gather an opcode-level trace when logs are insufficient. You will inspect Hardhat's stack trace output to extract the file name and line number where a revert happened, then follow the call stack to find which caller triggered the failure. Finally, you will practice test hygiene: ensure beforeEach resets state, always await asynchronous calls in your scripts and tests, and validate external contract responses when calls cross contract boundaries. Each card contains a simple mnemonic or micro-step you can follow during your debugging workflow so that you don’t conflate symptoms with root causes during investigation.

Smart contracts run on the EVM and their execution is transaction-based, so you can’t attach a conventional debugger to an on-chain process. That means your debugging toolbox must adapt: you need ways to observe values during a transaction and to reconstruct the execution history after a failure. Hardhat addresses both needs. It hosts a local EVM where tests and scripts run quickly, and it augments Solidity with a console logging utility that prints to your terminal during test execution. When a transaction reverts, Hardhat also produces a stack trace showing the sequence of function calls and the file and line where the revert occurred. For deeper analysis, the network can output a full transaction trace with every EVM opcode and gas usage, giving you a step-by-step replay. A practical takeaway is this: start with fast, low-overhead inspections like console prints to narrow suspect code paths. If those prints don’t reveal the root cause, escalate to stack traces and then to a verbose transaction trace to inspect opcodes and gas accounting. A common misconception is assuming an "out of gas" message always means your algorithm is expensive; sometimes a require consumed remaining gas and produced a revert. Always check the stack trace before concluding performance issues. How would you decide which tool to use first on a failing test?

Hardhat provides a simple debugging utility you can use directly inside Solidity: the console log import. After importing the console helper from Hardhat, you can call the print facility to output values to the terminal when running tests on Hardhat Network. This works much like printing in JavaScript: you can log strings and common types such as uint and address to observe state at specific moments in a transaction. The recommended pattern is to add prints right before a suspected failing check and immediately after calculations so you can see input, intermediate, and post-check values. Keep in mind console logs are intended for development only — they require the Hardhat environment and should not be left in production deployments. A common mistake is assuming console output is part of the transaction receipt; it is not. It appears in the running Hardhat terminal and interleaves with test output. Use console logs for quick hypothesis checks: if a printed value already shows the problem, you can often fix the logic without running a verbose trace. But if prints stop before revealing the cause, escalate to stack traces and verbose traces.

Let's walk through a concrete example so you can see console logging in action. Imagine a setValue function that logs the current value, the proposed new value, and the updated value. When you call it with a value that violates a require, you will see only the logs emitted before the require; any logs after the failing require don’t appear. In a test run you will notice log lines interleaved with test output, showing the printed values before failure. For example, calling setValue with 250 will print the current and proposed values and then the test output will show a revert with the reason string. This pattern helps you determine whether the error comes from the inputs, a calculation, or the require check itself. A frequent confusion is seeing logs and assuming state changed on-chain — remember the logs are local test output and state only persists if the transaction succeeded. Use console prints to confirm an assumption, then use a stack trace to point exactly at the failing line if prints don’t fully explain the issue. Example: setValue and visible console output means printed logs before a failing require reveal input and intermediate values, helping isolate the failing condition.. In practical terms, walk through a failing setvalue call and the printed output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Running your test suite is the normal entry point for debugging. Start with npx hardhat test. If a test fails and you used console prints, you’ll see those prints interleaved with Mocha and Hardhat test output in your terminal. If a transaction reverts, Hardhat will usually print an automatic stack trace showing where the revert happened. The practical process is: first run tests normally and observe printed logs. If you see a revert with a reason string, note the at-line that Hardhat prints; it includes the file name and line number. Second, if the cause remains unclear, rerun the same failing test with npx hardhat test --verbose to obtain a transaction trace with opcode-level detail. Third, when troubleshooting interactive state or running multiple steps, consider launching npx hardhat node and using the Hardhat console to invoke functions manually, inspect storage variables, and replay sequences that lead to the failure. A common mistake is skipping awaits in tests, which can make logs appear out of order or tests pass incorrectly. Always await transactions and deployments. This process ensures you escalate only as necessary, saving time while still giving you deep visibility when you need it.

Not all reverts come with a clear reason string. Some operations, such as a division by zero or an arithmetic error, produce a generic revert without a reason. When that happens, console logs can show you whether the divisor or operand values are what you expect, but if logs don’t show the failing operation, you need to inspect the stack trace. Hardhat’s stack trace will still point you to the file and line that triggered the revert, which is the primary clue to the underlying operation that failed. For example, if you call a divideByZero function with a 0 divisor, the transaction will revert and Hardhat will give a trace showing the divide instruction location. A common misconception is assuming a generic revert is always a compiler or EVM bug; usually it’s caused by an arithmetic or low-level operation in your code. If the failing line is inside an external call, trace the call stack to find the external contract and debug it similarly. The practical approach is first confirm inputs with console logs, then read the at-line in the stack trace, and finally escalate to verbose opcode traces when the issue involves low-level EVM behavior or unexpected gas consumption.

Hardhat enhances failing transactions with stack traces that reveal the sequence of function calls leading to a revert, including file names and line numbers. When you see an at-line such as contracts/BuggyContract. sol:21:9, the file and line tell you where the failing statement lives. The call stack shows which functions called which, helping you locate which caller passed a bad input or which nested call failed. The stack trace is your first stop after a revert because it points directly at the code location needing inspection. To interpret it, open the referenced file at the given line and examine the expression or require. Then trace backwards through the call stack to identify the caller that produced the input or state leading to the failure. Remember: the stack trace reports where the runtime error was detected, not necessarily where the original bad data was introduced. Use console logs in callers or earlier states to find where incorrect values were created. A common misunderstanding is thinking the topmost at-line is always the root cause; it’s the symptom location — you must use the call stack and prints to find the originating action.

When a failing transaction involves low-level behavior, unexpected gas consumption, or complex state changes, rerun your tests with npx hardhat test --verbose to produce a full transaction trace. The verbose trace shows every EVM opcode executed, gas costs per opcode, and changes to memory and storage. This level of detail is useful when diagnosing out-of-gas errors that are not simple require checks, investigating subtle storage overwrites, or verifying that external calls behaved as expected. Reading a verbose trace requires patience: look for the point where gas drops or where a REVERT opcode appears, then map that opcode back to the Solidity code using the line numbers and opcodes as clues. A practical approach is to first identify the failing Solidity line from the standard stack trace, then use the verbose opcode trace to inspect the precise EVM operations around that line. Remember that opcode traces are dense; use them as a microscope after your higher-level prints and traces have narrowed the suspect area. This staged escalation ensures you only dive into opcodes when necessary, saving time while still giving you the full fidelity needed to diagnose low-level issues.

For exploratory debugging you can start a local persistent node with npx hardhat node and then use the Hardhat console to interact with deployed contracts manually. This is useful when you want to step through a sequence of transactions, inspect storage between calls, or reproduce a failing scenario by invoking transactions one at a time. The typical flow is: launch the node, deploy your contracts to it through a script or by deploying from the console, then use the console prompt to call functions, check public storage values, and observe return values or reverts. Manual calls let you narrow down the problem by isolating a single step rather than running the whole test. There are several common pitfalls that slow down debugging. First, misinterpreting gas errors: an apparent out-of-gas can actually come from a require or revert that consumed remaining gas. Always inspect the stack trace before concluding a performance issue. Second, test state leakage: if your beforeEach doesn’t reset state properly, leftover state from a prior test can change behavior unexpectedly. Make sure each test deploys fresh contracts or otherwise resets shared state. Third, missing awaits: forgetting to await an asynchronous ethers. js call can cause subsequent steps to execute with unresolved promises, producing confusing failures or interleaved logs. Fourth, external call failures: when your contract calls another contract and the external call fails, the stack trace might show the revert inside the external contract; you must debug that dependency similarly. The practical strategy is to follow a checklist: run isolated tests, add prints to callers and callees, read the stack trace to find the failing line, and use verbose traces only if the cause remains unclear. Keeping these traps in mind will prevent many false leads and save debugging time.
